translations.text: Jesus said to his disciples, "I am the good shepherd," and so on.
This gospel, which has just been read, says that the Saviour said of himself, "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd gives his own life for his sheep.
The hireling, who is not the true shepherd, sees the wolf coming, and he abandons the sheep and flees; and the wolf seizes some and scatters the others," and so on.
Christ is good by nature, and truly nothing is good except God alone.
If any creature is good, then that goodness comes from the Creator, who is supremely good. He said, "The good shepherd gives his own life for his sheep."
Our Redeemer is the good shepherd, and we Christian people are his sheep, and he gave his own life for our redemption. He did just as he taught, and by that he showed what he commanded.
Peter was a good shepherd, and Paul was good, and the apostles were good, who gave their lives for God's people and for the true faith;
but their goodness came from the head, that is Christ, who is their head, and they are his limbs.
Every bishop and every teacher is set as a shepherd over God's people, so that they must shield the people against the wolf.
The wolf is the devil, who lays snares around God's church and watches for how he may destroy the souls of Christian people with sins.
Then the shepherd, that is, the bishop or another teacher, must withstand the fierce wolf with teaching and with prayers.
With teaching he must instruct them, so that they know what the devil teaches people to their ruin, and what God commands to be kept for the gaining of eternal life.
He must pray for them, that God may keep the strong and heal the weak.
He is counted among the strong who withstands the devil's teaching; he is weak who falls into sins.
But the teacher is guiltless if he guides the people with teaching and intercedes for them with God.
These two things he must do for the people, and also help them with his own other goods; and if it so happens, give his own life for the people's deliverance.

"The hireling flees when he sees the wolf." He is a hireling and not a shepherd who is caught up in worldly things, and loves the honour and the perishable rewards, and has no inward love for God's sheep.
He looks after the payments, and rejoices in the honour, and has his reward in this life, and is cut off from the eternal reward.
You do not know who is a hireling and who a shepherd before the wolf comes; but the wolf reveals with what mind he cared for the sheep.
The wolf comes to the sheep, and some he bites, some he scatters, when the fierce devil draws Christian people, some to fornication, [?]
some he kindles to greed, some he stirs up to pride, some he separates through anger, and with various temptations he slays them spiritually.
But the hireling is stirred neither by care nor by love, but flees, because he thinks about worldly gains and neglects the loss of the sheep.
He does not flee with his body, but with his mind. He flees because he saw injustice and kept silent.
He flees because he is a hireling and not a shepherd, as if it were said thus: he cannot stand against the dangers to the sheep,
he who does not care for the sheep with love, but looks after himself; that is, he loves earthly treasures, and not God's people.
The wolf is also the unrighteous rich man, who robs the Christians and oppresses the humble with his tyranny:
but the hireling, or the wage-earner, does not dare to withstand their wickedness, lest he lose his honour and the worldly riches which he loves more than the Christian people.
About this the prophet Ezekiel wrote, saying: "You shepherds, hear the word of God: My sheep are scattered through your negligence, and are devoured.
You care about your own food, and not about that of the sheep; therefore I will demand the sheep from your hands, and I will make you give up your office, and I will rescue my flock from you.
I myself will gather my sheep that were scattered, and I will keep them in abundant pasture: what was lost I will seek and lead back;
what was injured I will heal; the weak I will strengthen, and the strong I will keep, and I will pasture them in judgment and in righteousness."
God spoke these words through the prophet Ezekiel, concerning teachers and concerning his people. You must be zealous for your own need, even if it should happen that the teacher is negligent, [?]
and do as Christ taught: "If the teacher teaches well and sets a bad example, do as he teaches, and not according to the example he sets."
The Saviour said of himself, "I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and they know me." That is, I love them, and they love me. He who does not love truth has not yet known God.
But consider whether you are God's sheep, whether you have yet come to know him, whether you love him in truth.
He said, "Just as my Father knows me, and I know him, so I give my own life for my sheep."
He knows his Father through himself, and we know through him. By the love with which he was willing to die for mankind, by that he showed how greatly he loves his Father.
He said, "I have other sheep that are not of this flock, and those I must lead, and they will hear my voice, and there shall be one flock and one shepherd."
He said this in the land of Judea: there was one flock there, of those people in that nation who believed in God.
The other sheep are those who turn to God from all other lands; and Christ will bring them all into one flock in the eternal life.
There are many shepherds under Christ, and yet he alone is the Shepherd of them all, who lives and reigns with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, forever into eternity. Amen.
